“Küche” sounds roughly like “KÜ-kheh”, with a soft, hissing “ch” after ü (like the “h” in “huge”). Not “KOO-heh”!
mein, dein, sein = “mine, dine, zine”; but Miete, riesig, Bienen = a long “ee”.
An “h” after a vowel isn't pronounced, it just makes the vowel long: Stuhl = “shtool”, Kühlschrank = “KÜÜL-shrank”.
Each pronoun has its own possessive. They all take endings like “ein / eine / ein” (no ending in the masculine and neuter, -e in the feminine and plural):
Just like English “his” and “her”, German depends on the owner: “sein Haus” = HIS house, “ihr Haus” = HER house (or THEIR house). “Ihr Haus” with a capital letter = your house (formal).
“euer” drops the middle “e” when it takes an ending: euer Balkon, but eure Wohnung.
As with “ein” (chap. 5), in the accusative ONLY the masculine changes: -en.
In the dative (with mit, bei, von…): meinem / meiner / meinem / meinen: “vor unserem Haus”, “mit meiner Mutter”.
3. Es gibt = there is / there are
“Es gibt” says that something exists somewhere. It's ALWAYS followed by the accusative and doesn't change in the plural (unlike English “there is / there are”):
There's a balcony. / It has a balcony.
There are two chairs in the kitchen.
Is there a café around here?
With “Hier ist / Hier sind” you point to something specific: “Hier ist das Bad.” With “es gibt” you just say that it exists.
Ordinals: 1–19 take -t- (zweite, vierte, fünfte; irregular: erste, dritte, siebte), 20+ take -st- (zwanzigste). After “im” they take the ending -en: im dritten Stock.
Flat ads: “2-Zimmer-Wohnung, 55 m², 3. OG, Balkon, 850 € warm”. “warm” = including heating and bills; “kalt” = without. OG = Obergeschoss (upper floor), EG = ground floor.

The house on Kastanienallee is old. It's over a hundred years old. It has four floors, an inner courtyard with a big chestnut tree and no lift.
On the ground floor is Lena's bakery. On the first floor lives Mr Brandt with Fritz.

On the second floor lives the Nowak family from Poland: Piotr, his wife Kasia and their twins, Ola and Kuba. The twins are seven and very noisy. Their favourite game is called “running down the stairs”.
Mara now lives on the third floor. And on the fourth floor? That's where Mrs Hoffmann lives. Nobody ever sees her. You only hear her piano, every evening at nine.
One evening, Mara is sitting on her balcony listening to the piano. The music is sad and beautiful. The next morning she asks Mr Brandt.
Mr Brandt, who is Mrs Hoffmann? I never see her.
Margarete Hoffmann. She's ninety. She used to be a pianist, very well known in the GDR. She has lived here for sixty years. But now her legs are weak. The stairs are too much for her.
Lena brings her bread. And her son comes from Leipzig at weekends. But during the week she's alone.
In the afternoon, Mara knocks on the door on the fourth floor. For a long time nothing happens. Then a small woman with white hair and lively blue eyes opens the door.
Good afternoon, Mrs Hoffmann. I'm Mara, your new neighbour from the third floor. I'm a nurse. I hear your piano every evening. It's wonderful.
Mrs Hoffmann looks at Mara for a long time. Then she smiles: “Come in, child. Have a cup of tea with me. Do you like Chopin?”
Her flat is dark and full: books, sheet music, photos, and in the middle a big black grand piano. On the wall hangs a photo: a young woman at the piano, in front of a thousand people.
From that day on, Mara knocks on the fourth-floor door every Wednesday. She takes her blood pressure, brings her fruit from the market, and Mrs Hoffmann plays Chopin for her.
Warum geht Frau Hoffmann nicht raus?
Die Treppe ist zu viel für sie.
